cve_summary: kernel/signal.c in the Linux kernel before 2.6.39 allows local users to spoof the uid and pid of a signal sender via a sigqueueinfo system call.
commit_message:
Prevent rt_sigqueueinfo and rt_tgsigqueueinfo from spoofing the signal code

Userland should be able to trust the pid and uid of the sender of a
signal if the si_code is SI_TKILL.

Unfortunately, the kernel has historically allowed sigqueueinfo() to
send any si_code at all (as long as it was negative - to distinguish it
from kernel-generated signals like SIGILL etc), so it could spoof a
SI_TKILL with incorrect siginfo values.

Happily, it looks like glibc has always set si_code to the appropriate
SI_QUEUE, so there are probably no actual user code that ever uses
anything but the appropriate SI_QUEUE flag.

So just tighten the check for si_code (we used to allow any negative
value), and add a (one-time) warning in case there are binaries out
there that might depend on using other si_code values.

Signed-off-by: Julien Tinnes <jln@google.com>
Acked-by: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
docstring:
Summary: This function implements the system call `rt_sigqueueinfo`, which sends real-time signals to a specified process.

Parameters: 
- pid (pid_t): The process ID of the target process.
- sig (int): The signal number to be sent.
- uinfo (siginfo_t __user *): A pointer to user-space siginfo structure containing additional signal information.

Returns: 
- int: Returns 0 on success, or a negative error code indicating the failure reason (e.g., -EFAULT for a bad user pointer, -EPERM for permission errors).

Logic: The function first copies the siginfo structure from user space. It checks if the signal code is valid and ensures that the caller is not attempting to impersonate another process. If the checks pass, it sets the signal number in the siginfo structure and calls `kill_proc_info` to send the signal to the specified process.
